script.opening: (Anxious, embarrassed, avoids eye contact.) "I need an HIV test. I did something stupid a few days ago — unprotected — and I've been reading stuff online and I'm absolutely terrified I've caught HIV. Can you just test me now, today, and not tell anyone — especially not my parents? Will the test tell me for sure right now?"

facts.text: "I'd have to work it out. A few days. Maybe three?" If helped to work it out: Saturday night around 11 pm; now Tuesday morning — about 58 hours ago.

"Someone I didn't really know. I don't know if they've got anything. I'd rather tell the clinic the rest." Only if asked very sensitively and privately: a man in his twenties he met on an app; condomless anal sex, Jordan was the receptive partner. Doesn't know the man's HIV status. No condom split — none used.
"Yeah, I wanted to. I'd had a couple of drinks, that's all. Nothing like that." No drugs. No money or gifts. Not pressured.
"No. Just can't sleep." No rash, fever, sore throat, discharge or pain passing urine.
Well. No medicines, no allergies. Never had a sexual-health test. Not vaccinated against hepatitis B as far as he knows. Two previous partners (protected).
Lives with his parents; at sixth-form college. Parents don't know he's gay. Has a mobile and can get to the sexual-health clinic by bus.
"That I've definitely got it. That my life's over. And my parents finding out."

Frightened and ashamed; responds well to a calm, non-judgemental doctor. Surprised by PEP: "Today? Okay. I didn't know that existed." Asks: "So the test today will tell me?" and "So I have to wait six weeks to know?" and "Will they tell my parents?" If the doctor only books a routine test next week, accept it (the trap).

ice.ideas: "I've probably caught HIV, and a test today will tell me for sure."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror from what he has read; shame; his parents finding out about the test and his sexuality.
ice.expectations: "A test today, a definite answer, and nobody told."

cues: "A few days ago." — the exact timing matters (PEP within 72 hours).
"I'd rather tell the clinic the rest." — respect privacy while getting what's needed.

checkpoints.text: Provides non-judgemental care and clarifies CONFIDENTIALITY/competence — confidential care for a competent young person, encouraging but not forcing parental involvement, with safeguarding limits explained

Establishes the EXACT TIMING of exposure FIRST and recognises that within 72 HOURS, PEP assessment is URGENT — same-day referral to sexual health/A&E (ideally within 24h), where eligibility depends on the type of sex and the partner’s likely HIV status (BHIVA/BASHH 2021)

Explains the WINDOW PERIOD accurately — a 4th-generation laboratory test detects most infections by ~4 weeks and a negative at 45 days or later is conclusive (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020); a negative test before the window closes does not exclude infection, and home finger-prick antibody-only tests have a longer window

Takes a focused RISK history and offers a BROADER screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C if risk factors, hep B vaccination) and discusses realistic transmission risk and PrEP for the future
Keeps a SAFEGUARDING lens (consent, exploitation, coercion, vulnerability) and acts if concerns arise
Contains the online-amplified FEAR with calm, accurate information and realistic risk — reassuring without dismissing — and responds to shame non-judgementally
Explains the testing plan and confidentiality clearly so a frightened teenager trusts and engages

Safety-nets and follows up: PEP pathway if in window, repeat-testing timeline (HIV at 45 days, syphilis at about 12 weeks), STI/hepatitis results, condoms/PrEP/risk-reduction, safe contact and review — calm, accurate, confidential care

worked.txt: "You did absolutely the right thing coming in, and there’s no judgement here at all. Let’s sort this out together calmly — I think you’ll feel better once we have a plan."
"This is confidential — I won’t tell your parents. The only exception is if I were worried you were being harmed, and I’d talk to you first. Otherwise, it stays between us."

"The most important thing right now — exactly when did this happen? … If it’s within the last three days, there’s a medicine that can cut the chance of HIV taking hold, but it’s urgent, so I’d send you to the sexual-health clinic or A&E today, and they’d decide whether it’s right for you."

"On testing today — I’ll be honest: a test now can’t give you a guaranteed all-clear, because HIV takes a few weeks to show up. The lab test picks up most infections by about four weeks, and a negative 45 days after the encounter means you’re clear. The home finger-prick kits take longer to become reliable. A negative now wouldn’t fully reassure us yet — so we test now and again."

"While we’re at it, let’s check for other infections too — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, hepatitis B — and I can vaccinate you against hepatitis B. For what it’s worth, the chance from a single encounter is usually low, but we test properly rather than guess."

"I know the internet has terrified you — let’s replace that with facts and a plan. Here are condoms and info on a prevention medicine called PrEP for the future. Come back for the repeat test, and contact me anytime you’re worried. You’re handling this really responsibly."

f.learning: A frightened teenager requesting an HIV test after unprotected sex needs non-judgemental, confidential sexual-health care delivered with calm. He is entitled to confidential care as a competent young person — encourage but do not force involving a parent, and be clear about confidentiality’s safeguarding limits, as this trust enables honest risk assessment. The critical first step is establishing the EXACT timing of the exposure: if it was within 72 hours, assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is urgent and time-critical — refer same-day to sexual health or A&E, as PEP should start as soon as possible (ideally within 24 hours, never beyond 72), and whether it is recommended depends on the type of sex and the partner’s likely HIV status (BHIVA/BASHH 2021). Answer "will it tell me for sure now?" honestly: HIV tests have a window period — a 4th-generation antigen/antibody laboratory test detects about 95% of infections by 4 weeks and a negative result at 45 days or later is conclusive (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020), so a negative test done sooner does not exclude infection and must be repeated; antibody-only home finger-prick tests have a longer window, and syphilis is repeated at about 12 weeks. Take a focused risk history (type of exposure, partner status/risk, condom use, other partners, substances), offer a broader screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C if risk factors, with hepatitis B vaccination), calibrate the realistic (usually low) per-exposure transmission risk without dismissing the fear, and discuss PrEP for future risk. Keep a safeguarding lens (consent, exploitation, coercion, vulnerability) and act on concerns. Above all, contain the online-amplified fear with accurate information, a clear testing plan and a safety-net, providing condoms and risk-reduction advice — the emotional containment matters as much as the clinical plan.

knowledge.guideline: BHIVA/BASHH UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (2021) · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA adult HIV testing guidelines (2020) · BHIVA/BASHH PrEP guideline (2025) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 18 (hepatitis B) · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
knowledge.summary: Time comes first: PEP only works if started within 72 hours, so establish exactly when the exposure was. Then explain honestly that a test today cannot give a final answer, arrange testing now and after the window, and keep a young person’s care confidential and non-judgemental.

points.t: Start PEP as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, and not beyond 72 hours after exposure [1]. It is a 28-day course. It is not recommended for every exposure: the decision depends on the type of sex and the partner’s likely HIV status, and PEP is not needed if the partner is known to be on treatment with an undetectable viral load [1]. Send him the same day to a sexual-health clinic or, out of hours, the emergency department.

A fourth-generation laboratory (antigen and antibody) test detects about 95% of infections by 4 weeks and 99% by 45 days; a negative result at 45 days or later excludes HIV from that exposure [2]. A test sooner can be falsely negative, so test at baseline and repeat after the window. Antibody-only point-of-care and self-tests have a longer window. After PEP, the follow-up test is timed from the end of the course [1].

Offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs (sites by exposure), syphilis and HIV serology, and hepatitis B testing. Hepatitis C testing is targeted by risk. Offer hepatitis B vaccination to those at risk [4]. Repeat syphilis testing at about 12 weeks to cover its window [1].
The chance of HIV from a single exposure is low in most situations, and varies with the type of sex and whether the partner has untreated HIV. Say this without dismissing his fear.

He can consent to his own tests and treatment, and his confidentiality is his; encourage, but do not require, family involvement [5]. Under 18 is still a child for safeguarding, so ask about consent, pressure, alcohol or drugs, payment or gifts, and an older partner. Sexual-health services use a structured CSE screen for all under-18s [6].
Condoms, a discussion of PrEP for anyone at ongoing risk (available free through sexual-health clinics) [3], and hepatitis B vaccination. A clear plan helps contain the fear.

Alcohol or drugs, relationship context, family worries, sleep and anxiety, online reading.
Fourth-generation HIV test at baseline and 45 days; syphilis at baseline and about 12 weeks; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs; hepatitis B; hepatitis C by risk.
HIV exposure risk by act and partner; other STIs; anxiety driven by online reading; safeguarding concerns.
Establishes timing for PEP eligibility; screens for seroconversion symptoms; screens for exploitation or non-consent.
Possible HIV exposure a few days ago, near the 72-hour PEP limit, needing same-day assessment; low but real risk.

model.text: Hi Jordan, I’m Dr Lee. You did the right thing getting in touch. There’s no judgement here at all — let’s sort this out together. Tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Non-judgemental opening that addresses shame straight away

model.text: I need an HIV test. I did something stupid a few days ago — unprotected — and I’ve been reading stuff online and I’m terrified. Can you test me today and not tell anyone, especially my parents? Will it tell me for sure right now?

I’ll answer all of that. First: this is confidential. At 17 you can agree to your own tests, and I won’t tell your parents. The only exception would be if I thought you were being harmed, and I’d talk to you first.
model.why: Confidentiality and competence clarified early, with the safeguarding limit

model.text: Okay. Thanks.
The most important question: exactly when did this happen — which day, and roughly what time?
model.why: Establishes timing first, because PEP depends on it

model.text: I’d have to work it out. A few days. Maybe three?

That might be right at the edge. There’s a medicine called PEP that can stop HIV taking hold, but it only works if it’s started within 72 hours — and the sooner the better. So I’m not going to guess. While we’re talking, I’ll arrange for the sexual-health clinic to see you today. If you’re still inside the window, they’ll decide whether you need it.
model.why: Acts on possible PEP eligibility immediately with a same-day referral

model.text: Today? Okay. I didn’t know that existed.
The clinic will need to know what kind of sex it was and a bit about the other person, because that decides whether the medicine is recommended. Are you able to tell me anything about them?
model.why: Focused risk history, explained so it doesn’t feel intrusive

model.text: Someone I didn’t really know. I don’t know if they’ve got anything. I’d rather tell the clinic the rest.

That’s fine. Can I ask a few things I ask everyone your age? Was everything that happened something you wanted? Had you been drinking or taken anything? Was the other person much older, or was there any money or gifts involved?
model.why: Safeguarding screen: consent, substances, age gap, exchange

model.text: Yeah, I wanted to. I’d had a couple of drinks, that’s all. Nothing like that.
Thanks for being honest. Any symptoms since — sore throat, rash, fever, discharge or pain passing urine?
model.why: Screens for STI and seroconversion-type symptoms

model.text: No. Just can’t sleep.
You said the reading online has terrified you. What’s been going through your mind?
model.why: Explores the fear behind the request

model.text: That I’ve definitely got it. That my life’s over. And my parents finding out.
That’s a frightening place to be, and it makes sense you can’t sleep. Let me give you the facts, because they’re much less scary than what you’ve read.
model.why: Validates fear and signals a shift to accurate information

model.text: First, the chance of catching HIV from one encounter is usually low. It depends on the type of sex and whether the other person has untreated HIV — but for most single encounters it’s small. We still test properly rather than guess.
So the test today will tell me?

Honestly, not for certain yet. HIV takes a while to show up. The lab test we use picks up most infections by four weeks, and a negative result 45 days after the encounter means you’re clear. So we test now, and again after 45 days. If you take PEP, the clinic will time the repeat test from when you finish it.
model.why: Explains the window period accurately and sets expectations

model.text: So I have to wait six weeks to know?
For a final answer, yes, but you won’t be waiting on your own. And the home finger-prick kits online take longer to become reliable, so the clinic or a blood test here is better.
model.why: Acknowledges the hard wait and steers him from less reliable self-tests

model.text: Here’s the plan. Today, the sexual-health clinic assesses you for PEP and does a full check — HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Some tests need repeating later because they have their own windows, like syphilis at about 12 weeks. They can also vaccinate you against hepatitis B.
model.why: Full screen with repeat testing and hepatitis B vaccination

model.text: Will they tell my parents?
No. Sexual-health clinics are confidential, and they see people your age every day. They may ask some of the same safety questions I did — that’s routine.
model.why: Reassures on confidentiality and prepares him for the clinic’s own screen

model.text: Going forward, condoms protect against HIV and most other infections. And there’s a daily or event-based tablet called PrEP that prevents HIV, free from the clinic, if you think you might be at risk again. Would that be useful to talk about there?
model.why: Risk reduction and PrEP offered without moralising

model.text: Yeah. I didn’t know any of this.

If the clinic can’t fit you in today, go to A&E — they can start PEP. In the next few weeks, a flu-like illness with a rash, fever or sore throat needs a check, so tell the clinic or me. And if the worry is stopping you sleeping or getting on with life, come back and we’ll talk.
model.why: Fallback route for PEP, seroconversion symptoms and emotional safety-net

model.text: Okay.
Just to check it’s clear — what are you going to do after this call?
Go to the clinic today about PEP and tests, or A&E if they can’t see me. Test again after 45 days. Ask about PrEP. And it’s private.
Perfect. You’re handling this really responsibly. Anything else you want to ask?
model.why: Affirms him and shares the floor

social.t: Online searching often inflates risk. Shame and fear of parents can stop young people coming back for repeat tests; a non-judgemental first contact matters.
Alcohol commonly accompanies unplanned sex in young people. Discuss it without lecturing, as part of risk reduction.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8: a 16- or 17-year-old can consent to his own treatment. Gillick applies only to under-16s.

Confidential sexual-health care is essential for young people (GMC 0–18 years). Under 18 is still a child (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026); share information if there are signs of exploitation or abuse.

professional.t: Know how to get same-day PEP locally — sexual-health clinic in hours, emergency department out of hours — and do not delay by booking a routine GP test instead.
Sexual-health clinic records are held separately from GP records, which many young people find reassuring. Record the GP consultation accurately and without judgement.

community.t: Local sexual-health clinics (walk-in or same-day), young people’s services such as Brook, free condoms schemes, and PrEP through sexual-health clinics.

redFlags: Exposure within 72 hours — same-day PEP assessment
Non-consensual sex, an older partner, payment, drugs or coercion — safeguarding (and a sexual assault referral centre if assault is disclosed)
Seroconversion-type illness: fever, rash, sore throat, swollen glands
psychosocial: Alcohol or drugs at the time; other recent partners
Family relationships and fear of disclosure
Sleep, anxiety and the effect of online reading
ice: Concern: his life being over; his parents finding out
Expectation: a secret test today that gives a definite answer

playbook.diagnosis: “You’ve had a possible exposure, and the chance of HIV is usually low. Because it might still be inside 72 hours, I want you assessed today for a medicine that can prevent it. A test now can’t give a final answer; a negative at 45 days can.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “HIV tests are like a smoke alarm that needs a little time for smoke to build up. Test too early and it may stay quiet even if there’s a fire. After 45 days, the alarm is reliable.”

management.reflectIce: “The internet has convinced you your life is over. Let’s replace that with facts: the risk is usually low, there may be a medicine that helps, and in six or seven weeks you’ll have a definite answer.”
management.psychosocial: Confidential, non-judgemental care; routine safeguarding questions; alcohol and condoms discussed without moralising; support for anxiety while he waits.
sharedPlan: Same-day sexual-health clinic (or A&E) for PEP assessment
Baseline HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests; repeat HIV at 45 days and syphilis at about 12 weeks
Hepatitis B vaccination; condoms; PrEP discussion
safetyNet: A&E if the clinic cannot see him today
Fever, rash or sore throat in the coming weeks, or worsening anxiety — contact the clinic or practice

pitfalls.intro: Most candidates know what an HIV test is. The station is failed on timing — missing the PEP window — and on false reassurance about a test done too early, delivered to a frightened teenager who needs both facts and calm.

items.fail: Booking a routine blood test without asking exactly when the exposure happened.
items.why: PEP must start within 72 hours, preferably within 24 (BHIVA/BASHH 2021). A delay here is irreversible.
items.fix: Ask the exact day and time first; if it could be within 72 hours, arrange same-day assessment.

items.fail: “If today’s test is negative, you’re in the clear.”
items.why: A fourth-generation test is conclusive only from 45 days (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020). False reassurance may stop him retesting.
items.fix: “We test now, and a negative at 45 days means you’re clear.”

items.fail: Telling him PEP is automatic for any unprotected sex, or prescribing it yourself.
items.why: PEP is recommended or considered depending on the act and the partner’s likely status, and is started by sexual-health or emergency services.
items.fix: Explain that the clinic decides, and get him there today.

items.fail: Lecturing about condoms or alcohol, or suggesting he tells his parents.
items.why: “Appeared judgemental”; at 17 he can consent and is entitled to confidentiality.
items.fix: Affirm that he came in, and discuss prevention as options for the future.

items.fail: Skipping the safeguarding questions because he is nearly 18 and male.
items.why: Under 18 is a child for safeguarding; exploitation affects boys too.
items.fix: Ask about consent, substances, age gap and payment, framed as routine.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll let you know the results” and no plan for repeat tests or PEP out of hours.
items.fix: A&E if the clinic can’t see him, repeat HIV at 45 days, syphilis at about 12 weeks, and seroconversion symptoms named.

timeMap.d: No judgement. Confidentiality at 17, and its safeguarding limit.
Exact timing first — within 72 hours means same-day PEP assessment. Type of exposure, partner, consent, substances, symptoms.
Online-driven terror, fear for his future, fear of parents finding out.
Realistic risk. Window period: 4th-generation test, repeat at 45 days. Full STI screen, hepatitis B vaccine, condoms, PrEP.
A&E if the clinic can’t see him today; seroconversion symptoms; repeat tests; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Takes a blood test and says “we’ll ring you with the result” without asking when the exposure was; implies a negative today means he is clear; moralises; tells him his parents should know.
wordPics.pass: Asks timing first and recognises the PEP window; explains the window period; arranges a full STI screen; keeps it confidential; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: acts on uncertain timing by arranging same-day assessment rather than guessing; knows PEP is not for every exposure; gives accurate numbers (45 days) in plain words; screens safeguarding as routine; offers hepatitis B vaccination and PrEP; turns terror into a plan he can repeat back.

avoid.dont: “We’ll do a test today and if it’s negative you’re fine.”
avoid.instead: “A test today can’t give a final answer. We test now and again at 45 days.”
avoid.why: False reassurance from a test inside the window period is a safety error.

avoid.dont: “Let’s book you in next week for bloods.”
avoid.instead: “If this was within 72 hours, there’s a medicine that can help, so I want you seen today.”
avoid.why: Missing the PEP window cannot be undone.

avoid.dont: “You really should have used a condom.”
avoid.instead: “You’ve done the right thing coming in. Let’s talk about what protects you next time.”
avoid.why: Moralising adds shame and makes him less likely to return for repeat testing.

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s the plan. Today, the sexual-health clinic assesses you for PEP and does a full check — HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Some tests need repeating later because they have their own windows, like syphilis at about 12 weeks. They can also vaccinate you against hepatitis B.
SCA_MODELS.why: Full screen with repeat testing and hepatitis B vaccination

SCA_MODELS.text: Will they tell my parents?
No. Sexual-health clinics are confidential, and they see people your age every day. They may ask some of the same safety questions I did — that’s routine.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reassures on confidentiality and prepares him for the clinic’s own screen

SCA_MODELS.text: Going forward, condoms protect against HIV and most other infections. And there’s a daily or event-based tablet called PrEP that prevents HIV, free from the clinic, if you think you might be at risk again. Would that be useful to talk about there?
SCA_MODELS.why: Risk reduction and PrEP offered without moralising

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. I didn’t know any of this.

If the clinic can’t fit you in today, go to A&E — they can start PEP. In the next few weeks, a flu-like illness with a rash, fever or sore throat needs a check, so tell the clinic or me. And if the worry is stopping you sleeping or getting on with life, come back and we’ll talk.
SCA_MODELS.why: Fallback route for PEP, seroconversion symptoms and emotional safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Just to check it’s clear — what are you going to do after this call?
Go to the clinic today about PEP and tests, or A&E if they can’t see me. Test again after 45 days. Ask about PrEP. And it’s private.
Perfect. You’re handling this really responsibly. Anything else you want to ask?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms him and shares the floor

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: BHIVA/BASHH UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (2021) · BHIVA/BASHH/BIA adult HIV testing guidelines (2020) · BHIVA/BASHH PrEP guideline (2025) · UKHSA Green Book chapter 18 (hepatitis B) · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Time comes first: PEP only works if started within 72 hours, so establish exactly when the exposure was. Then explain honestly that a test today cannot give a final answer, arrange testing now and after the window, and keep a young person’s care confidential and non-judgemental.

points.t: Start PEP as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, and not beyond 72 hours after exposure [1]. It is a 28-day course. It is not recommended for every exposure: the decision depends on the type of sex and the partner’s likely HIV status, and PEP is not needed if the partner is known to be on treatment with an undetectable viral load [1]. Send him the same day to a sexual-health clinic or, out of hours, the emergency department.

A fourth-generation laboratory (antigen and antibody) test detects about 95% of infections by 4 weeks and 99% by 45 days; a negative result at 45 days or later excludes HIV from that exposure [2]. A test sooner can be falsely negative, so test at baseline and repeat after the window. Antibody-only point-of-care and self-tests have a longer window. After PEP, the follow-up test is timed from the end of the course [1].

Offer chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs (sites by exposure), syphilis and HIV serology, and hepatitis B testing. Hepatitis C testing is targeted by risk. Offer hepatitis B vaccination to those at risk [4]. Repeat syphilis testing at about 12 weeks to cover its window [1].
The chance of HIV from a single exposure is low in most situations, and varies with the type of sex and whether the partner has untreated HIV. Say this without dismissing his fear.

He can consent to his own tests and treatment, and his confidentiality is his; encourage, but do not require, family involvement [5]. Under 18 is still a child for safeguarding, so ask about consent, pressure, alcohol or drugs, payment or gifts, and an older partner. Sexual-health services use a structured CSE screen for all under-18s [6].
Condoms, a discussion of PrEP for anyone at ongoing risk (available free through sexual-health clinics) [3], and hepatitis B vaccination. A clear plan helps contain the fear.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Non-judgemental open question; hears his three questions (test today, secrecy, certainty) and answers each.
Alcohol or drugs, relationship context, family worries, sleep and anxiety, online reading.
Picks up “a few days ago” (PEP window), “will it tell me for sure?” and “especially not my parents”.
Idea: he has probably caught HIV; concern: his life is over and his parents finding out; expectation: a secret, definitive test today.
Fourth-generation HIV test at baseline and 45 days; syphilis at baseline and about 12 weeks; chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs; hepatitis B; hepatitis C by risk.
HIV exposure risk by act and partner; other STIs; anxiety driven by online reading; safeguarding concerns.
Establishes timing for PEP eligibility; screens for seroconversion symptoms; screens for exploitation or non-consent.
Possible HIV exposure a few days ago, near the 72-hour PEP limit, needing same-day assessment; low but real risk.
Same-day sexual-health or A&E for PEP assessment; honest window-period explanation; full STI screen; hepatitis B vaccination; confidentiality kept.
Alcohol and risk-taking discussed without moralising; condoms; PrEP; anxiety addressed.
A&E fallback for PEP; seroconversion symptoms; repeat tests at 45 days and about 12 weeks; return if anxiety persists.

social.t: Online searching often inflates risk. Shame and fear of parents can stop young people coming back for repeat tests; a non-judgemental first contact matters.
Alcohol commonly accompanies unplanned sex in young people. Discuss it without lecturing, as part of risk reduction.

legal.t: Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8: a 16- or 17-year-old can consent to his own treatment. Gillick applies only to under-16s.

Confidential sexual-health care is essential for young people (GMC 0–18 years). Under 18 is still a child (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026); share information if there are signs of exploitation or abuse.

professional.t: Know how to get same-day PEP locally — sexual-health clinic in hours, emergency department out of hours — and do not delay by booking a routine GP test instead.
Sexual-health clinic records are held separately from GP records, which many young people find reassuring. Record the GP consultation accurately and without judgement.

community.t: Local sexual-health clinics (walk-in or same-day), young people’s services such as Brook, free condoms schemes, and PrEP through sexual-health clinics.

redFlags: Exposure within 72 hours — same-day PEP assessment
Non-consensual sex, an older partner, payment, drugs or coercion — safeguarding (and a sexual assault referral centre if assault is disclosed)
Seroconversion-type illness: fever, rash, sore throat, swollen glands
psychosocial: Alcohol or drugs at the time; other recent partners
Family relationships and fear of disclosure
Sleep, anxiety and the effect of online reading
ice: Concern: his life being over; his parents finding out
Expectation: a secret test today that gives a definite answer

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’ve had a possible exposure, and the chance of HIV is usually low. Because it might still be inside 72 hours, I want you assessed today for a medicine that can prevent it. A test now can’t give a final answer; a negative at 45 days can.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “HIV tests are like a smoke alarm that needs a little time for smoke to build up. Test too early and it may stay quiet even if there’s a fire. After 45 days, the alarm is reliable.”

management.reflectIce: “The internet has convinced you your life is over. Let’s replace that with facts: the risk is usually low, there may be a medicine that helps, and in six or seven weeks you’ll have a definite answer.”
management.psychosocial: Confidential, non-judgemental care; routine safeguarding questions; alcohol and condoms discussed without moralising; support for anxiety while he waits.

Baseline HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, chlamydia and gonorrhoea tests; repeat HIV at 45 days and syphilis at about 12 weeks
Hepatitis B vaccination; condoms; PrEP discussion
safetyNet: A&E if the clinic cannot see him today

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Most candidates know what an HIV test is. The station is failed on timing — missing the PEP window — and on false reassurance about a test done too early, delivered to a frightened teenager who needs both facts and calm.

items.fail: Booking a routine blood test without asking exactly when the exposure happened.
items.why: PEP must start within 72 hours, preferably within 24 (BHIVA/BASHH 2021). A delay here is irreversible.
items.fix: Ask the exact day and time first; if it could be within 72 hours, arrange same-day assessment.

items.fail: “If today’s test is negative, you’re in the clear.”
items.why: A fourth-generation test is conclusive only from 45 days (BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020). False reassurance may stop him retesting.
items.fix: “We test now, and a negative at 45 days means you’re clear.”

items.fail: Telling him PEP is automatic for any unprotected sex, or prescribing it yourself.
items.why: PEP is recommended or considered depending on the act and the partner’s likely status, and is started by sexual-health or emergency services.
items.fix: Explain that the clinic decides, and get him there today.

items.fail: Lecturing about condoms or alcohol, or suggesting he tells his parents.
items.why: “Appeared judgemental”; at 17 he can consent and is entitled to confidentiality.
items.fix: Affirm that he came in, and discuss prevention as options for the future.

items.fail: Skipping the safeguarding questions because he is nearly 18 and male.
items.why: Under 18 is a child for safeguarding; exploitation affects boys too.
items.fix: Ask about consent, substances, age gap and payment, framed as routine.

items.fail: Ending with “we’ll let you know the results” and no plan for repeat tests or PEP out of hours.
items.fix: A&E if the clinic can’t see him, repeat HIV at 45 days, syphilis at about 12 weeks, and seroconversion symptoms named.
